Appendix B. Time-of-Use Rates and Price-Responsive Dispatch For the TOU dispatch mechanism modeled in the main text, we construct TOU rates that attempt to mimic hourly RTP patterns as closely as possible while enforcing a season and block structure. Seasons, defined as a set of contiguous days, and blocks, defined as a set of contiguous hours, are chosen because these commonly feature in retail TOU prices with on-peak, mid peak, and/or off-peak rates that vary by season and times of day. Although our optimization formulation is general and could be used to construct any number of rates with different numbers of seasons, blocks, and restrictions on season and block length, in this study we analyze a TOU rate with one season and two blocks. The TOU rate we construct is intended to represent only the wholesale energy portion of a typical retail tariff. Other common retail tariff components other than wholesale energy include distribution, transmission, and line items to cover specific utility programs; these costs are not reflected in our rates except to the extent transmission congestion is captured in nodal PLEXOS simulations. Based on our modeling framework, we derive the wholesale energy portion of rates from the hourly real-time prices in the day-ahead PLEXOS model with unmanaged EV charging loads. Seasons are defined as groups of contiguous days that can wrap around the first day of the year (i.e., December 31 and January 1 can be in the same season). Blocks are defined separately for weekdays and weekend days, but in both cases, they consist of groups of contiguous hours that can wrap around at midnight (i.e., 11 p.m.–12 a.m. and 12 a.m.–1 a.m. can be in the same block). Seasons must persist for a minimum number of days (not applicable to our 1-season TOU rate); blocks must be at least as long as a minimum number of hours (4 in our TOU rate). The resulting TOU rate used in this study is in Table A.1. Consistent with average wholesale energy costs, TOU rates are lower overnight than in the daytime and are lower on the weekend than on weekdays. For both weekends and weekdays, lower rates start at midnight. The transition to daytime prices happens at 7 a.m. on weekdays and at 9 a.m. on weekends.
